parts: Lesson 5: Tissues and Other Levels of Organization — Summary

A tissue is a group of cells with a common origin, structure and function; the study of tissues is histology. Several tissues form an organ (e.g. blood, bone and cartilage in animals; parenchyma, collenchyma, xylem and phloem in plants).

Meristematic tissues: undifferentiated, living, thin-walled cells with dense cytoplasm, a prominent nucleus, small or no vacuoles and no intercellular spaces; they keep dividing. Apical meristem (root and shoot tips) increases length; intercalary meristem (at the bases of leaves or internodes) causes internodal growth and growth of leaf in grasses; lateral meristem (cambium and cork cambium) increases thickness (secondary growth). Permanent tissues have stopped dividing, and are simple (one type of cell) or complex (more than one type of cell working as a unit).

Simple tissues: parenchyma (living, thin-walled, oval or round cells with intercellular spaces; stores food; chlorenchyma carries out photosynthesis and aerenchyma has air spaces to give buoyancy in aquatic plants; found in cortex, pith, mesophyll, endosperm); collenchyma (living, with cellulose and pectin thickening at the corners; gives mechanical support and flexibility to young stems, petioles and leaves); sclerenchyma (dead, thick lignified walls; fibres and sclereids; gives strength and protection). Complex tissues: xylem (conducts water and minerals upward; made of tracheids, vessels, fibres and xylem parenchyma; all except parenchyma are dead) and phloem (conducts the food made in the leaves to other parts; made of sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem fibres and phloem parenchyma; sieve tubes and companion cells are living).

Tunica-corpus theory (for the shoot apex): the tunica is the peripheral layers showing anticlinal division and giving surface growth (epidermis and cortex); the corpus is the central mass with irregular division giving volume (pith and vascular tissue). Histogen theory: the promeristem differentiates into dermatogen (epidermis in the stem, epiblema in the root), periblem (cortex) and plerome (pericycle, pith and vascular tissue).
Four types: epithelial (protection by covering, secretion, absorption), connective (binding and support), muscular (movement) and nervous (control and coordination).

Epithelial tissue: closely packed cells without intercellular spaces, resting on a non-cellular basement membrane, with no blood vessels. Types: squamous (flat cells; lining of lung air sacs and blood capillaries; exchange), cuboidal (cube-shaped; kidney tubules, glands; secretion and absorption), columnar (stomach and intestine lining; secretion and absorption), ciliated columnar (lining of trachea; moves mucus in one direction), brush-bordered columnar (intestine lining; the folds increase the surface for absorption); compound or stratified epithelium (many layers) is found where there is wear and tear (skin, lining of cheeks).

Connective tissue has a matrix and cells. Proper: areolar (fibroblasts form collagen and elastin fibres; macrophages engulf bacteria; mast cells release heparin), adipose (stores fat) and fibrous (tendons and ligaments). Supporting: cartilage (matrix of chondrin) and bone (matrix of ossein with calcium and phosphorus salts; Haversian system in compact bone, spongy bone at the ends of long bones; bone marrow makes blood cells). Fluid: blood (plasma, RBCs for gas transport, WBCs for defence, platelets for clotting; plasma proteins are fibrinogen, albumin and globulin) and lymph.

Muscle tissue (contractile proteins actin, myosin, troponin, tropomyosin): striated (skeletal, voluntary; cylindrical, unbranched, multinucleate fibres), unstriated (smooth, involuntary; spindle-shaped, uninucleate; in walls of stomach and intestine) and cardiac (involuntary, striated, branched with intercalated discs; in the heart). Nervous tissue: neurons (cell body with dendrites and an axon) and neuroglia; it conducts impulses.
